title: MOSAIQC: Mixed-topology-aware Optimization for Scalable Approximate noise-Informed Quantum circuit Cutting
authors: Koen Mesman, Yinglu Tang, Matthias Moller, Boyang Chen, Sebastian Feld
abstract: Current quantum computers do not yet have the required qubit resources to meet the demands of most practical quantum algorithms. To circumvent this constraint, the practice of dividing these algorithms into parts through quantum circuit cutting has been explored. Many of these works either show exponential scaling or are far from optimal solutions. In this paper, MosaiQC is presented as a novel framework to improve upon existing circuit cutting frameworks. A hybrid warmstart with refinement optimization is used to find cutting solutions, allowing the combination of both wire and gate cuts. Additionally, MosaiQC enables hardware partitions of mixed sizes. Furthermore, the refinement stage incorporates a fast approximate quadratic assignment solver to better place hardware partitions, demonstrating a mean local fidelity improvement of $19.56 \% \pm 6.17\%$ over the baseline algorithm. In runtime and sampling overhead costs, improvements of $2.88 \times$ and an average of $16.84\%$ cut reduction (resulting in an average $5.83 \cdot 10^{11} \times$ overhead reduction) are observed. MosaiQC demonstrates a superior trade-off for run speed and solution quality, while adding fundamental features excluded by most competitors. With this, MosaiQC demonstrates that scalable heuristic optimization can substantially reduce the computational overhead of circuit-cut placement for increasingly large quantum circuits.
summary: This paper introduces MOSAIQC, a novel framework designed to overcome limitations in running large quantum algorithms on current noisy hardware by intelligently cutting and remapping circuits. It achieves this through a hybrid optimization process that jointly considers gate/wire cuts, hardware noise profiles, and sampling overhead. The results show substantial improvements in both speed and solution quality compared to existing methods.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a scalable method for quantum circuit cutting to execute large algorithms on current, resource-limited Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware.
main_result: MOSAIQC demonstrates superior trade-offs in run speed and solution quality by jointly optimizing sampling overhead, hardware placement, and mixed gate/wire cuts, achieving significant reductions in computational overhead.
method: The framework uses a hybrid approach combining global heuristics (like METIS) for initial partitioning with local refinement optimization (Tabu Search), incorporating noise-informed cost functions.
model_or_system: The system involves mapping large quantum circuits onto smaller, potentially heterogeneous quantum processors. The circuit connectivity and hardware topology are modeled as weighted graphs to calculate cutting costs.
key_observables: Local fidelity improvement (+19.56% $\pm$ 6.17%), runtime speedup ($2.88 	imes$), and massive reduction in sampling overhead ($	ext{average } 5.83 \cdot 10^{11}	imes$).
important_parameters: Qubit count (scaling from 6 to 1000+), cut types (gate vs. wire), hardware connectivity, and noise characteristics.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the ability to convert quantum circuit objects into lightweight graph structures for efficient computation; existing heuristics often fail to jointly optimize all necessary parameters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate performance comparisons across various benchmark circuits (e.g., QAOA, Ising VQE) at increasing qubit scales, showing runtime and sampling overhead results for different cut placement strategies.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of circuit cutting limitations, details the novel MOSAIQC framework using graph representations and a hybrid optimization strategy, presents specific algorithms for wire/gate cut cost calculation, and concludes with extensive comparative results across multiple scales and benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous development of scalable heuristic optimization techniques for resource allocation (like circuit partitioning) shares methodological parallels with optimizing complex physical simulations or network mapping in AMO physics.
